name: やまだ屋 宮島本店 (Yamadaya Miyajima Honten)

claims.text: Signature products (momiji manju, kiriyoka) are wheat-flour cakes made in a shared confectionery production environment; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Momiji manju is an egg-based castella cake; no vegan products or egg/dairy-free handling are documented.
Anagomeshi and the rice bowls are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce/tare, which contains wheat; udon is also wheat-based.
Kitchen centers on conger eel, oysters, eggs, and fish-based dashi, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable across the menu.
Anago is finished with a wheat-based soy-sauce tare and udon is a wheat noodle, so gluten is present throughout the core menu; no GF handling is documented.
The anagomeshi glaze/seasoning is soy-sauce based, which in Japan is typically brewed with wheat.
Kitchen centers on conger eel and oysters; no vegan-safe preparation indicated.
Edomae nigiri is conventionally brushed with nikiri (a wheat-based soy sauce reduction); no gluten-free soy sauce is documented for this restaurant.

name: 湯葉と豆腐の店 梅の花 広島店 (Yuba to Tofu no Mise Ume no Hana Hiroshima-t)

claims.text: Soy-sauce-based seasonings and wheat-battered fried yuba/tempura items are used throughout the kitchen, so gluten cross-contact is likely; the restaurant does not list wheat among the allergens it can accommodate.
Kaiseki dishes use standard Japanese soy sauce and dashi, which typically contain wheat.
Tofu and yuba dishes share a kitchen with seafood, egg, and dairy preparations; standard dashi may contain fish, so plant-only diners should request accommodation in advance.

Allergy accommodation is offered only on a limited basis to guests who reserve in advance, and only for eggs, dairy, buckwheat, peanuts, crab, shrimp, and walnuts; allergens outside that list cannot be handled.
The core ingredients are house-made tofu and freshly pulled yuba, so plant-forward diners have genuinely soy-centered options to build a meal around when they arrange it ahead.

Menu is built around matcha, fruit-syrup shaved ice, and red-bean zenzai rather than fried or heavy wheat-based dishes, which can give plant-based or wheat-avoiding diners a starting point to ask about.

name: ゆかりんの台所 (Yukarin no Daidokoro)

claims.text: Menu includes a herb-butter soy-flavored beef steak; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so soy-seasoned dishes here should be assumed to contain gluten.
The kitchen uses fresh organic vegetables from contracted farmers, so plant-forward sides may be available on request.
Oden ingredients including wheat-gluten 車麩 are simmered together in shared communal pots, so even non-wheat items share the same broth.
The 'black dashi' and stewed dishes use 大野醤油 (Oono soy sauce), a traditional whole-soybean soy sauce that contains wheat.
The base white dashi is made from kombu and dried sardines (niboshi), so all simmered items, including vegetables, sit in fish stock.
